01
The play

One format, repeated until it became a habit.

Before launch, Briefly had a waitlist and no product in stores. The job for the summer was to build an audience that already trusted us when the app arrived. We picked one repeatable unit, the seven-slide carousel, and gave every slide a single job.

02
Method

Design it by hand. Teach it. Then let it run.

Two carousels a day is too many to hand-design for a three-person founding team. So the summer became a process of turning taste into instructions an AI could follow without losing the voice.

STAGE 01

Hand-design all seven

We built the first carousels slide by slide to find what worked: the hook length, where the evidence goes, which slide earns the save, and how the call to action should land.

June
STAGE 02

Teach the AI

Every rule we learned became a written skill: a copywriter, a layout generator, an exporter, and an illustration style guide. The AI now drafts complete carousels in our format and voice.

July
STAGE 03

Ship explainer carousels

With production solved, the content became the focus: memory science, curated podcast lists, and Briefly feature highlights, told through a recurring illustrated character.

August to September
03
Three pillars

Why listen, what to hear, how Briefly helps.

Every carousel belonged to one of three content pillars. Together they tell one story: podcasts are a powerful way to learn, here is where to start, and Briefly makes the best parts easy to reach.

Why listening helps you remember.

A cognitive science angle on why podcasts stick, and why short, real clips fit how memory actually works. Each carousel took one research finding and made it visual.

  • Retrieval beats rereading. People who practice recalling an idea keep far more of it a week later than people who just review it again.
  • Voice carries meaning. Listeners judge a speaker as more thoughtful when they hear the words instead of reading them, which is why we clip and never summarize.
  • Attention is short. Screen attention now lasts under a minute, so a five-minute brief meets people where they are.
  • Load and curiosity. Cognitive load theory and the information gap explained why one idea per slide, and a hook that opens a question, outperform dense recaps.

A curated list for every skill.

The Podcast Recs series ran every other day: a cover, ranked shows with the exact episode to start with, and a call to action. Lists are the format people save, so this pillar fed the save rate.

  • By skill. Leadership, money, health, mindset, and business, each with episodes picked for one outcome.
  • By episode, not by show. We named the guest and the episode, so the list is useful the moment it is saved.
  • Big and niche together. Household names like The Diary of a CEO and Acquired sit next to smaller shows people would not find alone.
  • Time-boxed hooks. "Five podcasts if you only have 20 minutes a day" sold the list on respect for time.

The product, one feature at a time.

Feature carousels showed what Briefly does without sounding like an ad. Each one started from a listener problem and ended on the feature that solves it.

  • Hours into minutes. A four-hour episode becomes a five to fifteen minute brief, in the host's own voice.
  • Made for you. Out of every new episode each week, only a few touch your work or curiosity. Briefly finds those.
  • Real people, not summaries. Why we kept the voice that AI summaries delete.
  • Follow to get in early. Every feature carousel closed on the waitlist.
04
Design evolution

From text on a card to a character with a job.

The look changed three times over the summer. Pick an era, browse the real slides, and open each design decision to see why it was made.

Side by side

Drag across the slide to compare eras on the same kind of message.

XiaoheiChibi

What changed, and what stayed.

The structure never moved: a hook, one idea per slide, a save-worthy slide near the end, and a follow call to action. What changed was everything around it. Texture, glow, and baked-in decoration came out. A single character, a flat white page, and a clear left-aligned reading line came in.

The result is a feed that reads as one series, where any slide is recognizably ours before the handle is visible.

Every tool in the chain, and the one job it does.

Claude, with custom skillsBrain of the pipeline

Copywriting, layout, illustration direction, and export, each written down as a reusable skill.

HiggsfieldIllustration

Generates every slide image from a locked style guide and a character reference.

Playwright + PillowExport

Renders slides to 1080 by 1350 PNGs, plus square and story crops.

GmailDelivery

Each carousel arrives as one email with a zip of slides and captions, labeled by date and time slot.

InstagramPublishing

Posted as a carousel with trending audio and per-slide captions, with collab invites to both founders.

ManyChatConversion

Commenting "Briefly" triggers a DM that leads to the waitlist and niche podcast lists.

What's next

After launch, we take it to the street.

Carousels earned attention for an idea. With the app live, organic marketing shifts to street interviews: real people, real reactions, and a product they can download the same day.
